scenes.tts: Adult rodents make new neurons. Do adult humans make them too?
scenes.visual: Title card: Do You Make Them Too? A human brain, hippocampus highlighted.
scenes.narration: Adult rodents make new neurons. Do adult humans make them too?

scenes.tts: B R D U cannot be given to healthy people for research.
scenes.caption: BrdU cannot be given to healthy people for research.
scenes.visual: A crossed-out syringe beside a healthy person icon.
scenes.narration: BrdU cannot be given to healthy people for research.

scenes.tts: But in the nineteen nineties, some cancer patients received it for clinical reasons.
scenes.caption: But in the 1990s, some cancer patients received it for clinical reasons.
scenes.visual: A clinical chart icon. Label: patients with cancer, 1990s.
scenes.narration: But in the 1990s, some cancer patients received it for clinical reasons.

scenes.tts: After death, their dentate gyrus held cells with both B R D U and a neuron protein. Both facts, in single human cells.
scenes.caption: After death, their dentate gyrus held cells with both BrdU and a neuron protein. Both facts, in single human cells.
scenes.visual: A human dentate gyrus cell stained in two overlapping colours, BrdU and NeuN. The two-fact card, both boxes ticked.
scenes.narration: After death, their dentate gyrus held cells with both BrdU and a neuron protein. Both facts, in single human cells.

scenes.tts: Bomb tests in the nineteen fifties and early sixties sharply raised the carbon fourteen in the air.
scenes.caption: Bomb tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the carbon-14 in the air.
scenes.visual: Schematic bomb curve, northern hemisphere: atmospheric carbon-14 against year, rising to a peak, then falling after a marker at 1963. Labelled schematic.
scenes.narration: Bomb tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the carbon-14 in the air.

scenes.tts: That carbon ends up in the DNA of dividing cells. A neuron's DNA keeps the level of its last division.
scenes.visual: Carbon passes through plants and food into a dividing cell's DNA; a neuron's DNA drops onto the curve at the year of its last division.
scenes.narration: That carbon ends up in the DNA of dividing cells. A neuron's DNA keeps the level of its last division.

scenes.tts: Neurons at the back of the cortex match the person's own birth year. They were born around then. So were olfactory bulb neurons.
scenes.visual: A donor's birth year marked on the curve; cortex and olfactory bulb readings sit on it.
scenes.narration: Neurons at the back of the cortex match the person's own birth year. They were born around then. So were olfactory bulb neurons.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Hippocampal neurons do not match the birth year. What can you conclude, and what not?
scenes.visual: Question card. A hippocampus reading sits off the curve at the birth year.
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Hippocampal neurons do not match the birth year. What can you conclude, and what not?

scenes.tts: An offset beyond measurement error points to neurons added after birth, unless repair or stray nuclei explain it. But a sample averages many nuclei, so it cannot say how many, or when.
scenes.visual: Many nuclei pour into one test tube, giving a single averaged reading. Caption: how many, and when? Needs a model.
scenes.narration: An offset beyond measurement error points to neurons added after birth, unless repair or stray nuclei explain it. But a sample averages many nuclei, so it cannot say how many, or when.

scenes.tts: One model estimate is about seven hundred new neurons per hippocampus per day.
scenes.caption: One model estimate is about 700 new neurons per hippocampus per day.
scenes.visual: On screen: about 700 new neurons per hippocampus per day. Model estimate.
scenes.narration: One model estimate is about 700 new neurons per hippocampus per day.

scenes.tts: Stains for young neurons show a state, not a birth date. In people, it is debated whether they mark only new neurons.
scenes.visual: A three-row method table builds: birth record, neuron identity, same cells. Rows: BrdU in patients, carbon-14, DCX staining.
scenes.narration: Stains for young neurons show a state, not a birth date. In people, it is debated whether they mark only new neurons.

scenes.tts: And the stains disagree. One study found none in adults. Others found thousands.
scenes.visual: Two panels: none in adults; thousands into old age.
scenes.narration: And the stains disagree. One study found none in adults. Others found thousands.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Suppose seven hundred new neurons arrive each day, and each stays young and marked for weeks or months. How many marked cells should one hippocampus hold?
scenes.visual: Question card: a steady 700 a day, each young and marked for weeks or months. How many at once?
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Suppose 700 new neurons arrive each day, and each stays young and marked for weeks or months. How many marked cells should one hippocampus hold?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Suppose 700 new neurons arrive each day, and each stays young and marked for weeks or months. How many marked cells should one hippocampus hold?

scenes.tts: Rate times time. Even three weeks gives about fifteen thousand across one hippocampus. These are toy numbers.
scenes.visual: Rate-times-time graphic: 700 a day flowing into a young box. On screen: 3 weeks, about 15,000; 3 months, 63,000; 6 months, 126,000. Label: toy numbers, steady rate assumed.
scenes.narration: Rate times time. Even three weeks gives about 15,000 across one hippocampus. These are toy numbers.
scenes.caption: Rate times time. Even three weeks gives about 15,000 across one hippocampus. These are toy numbers.

scenes.tts: So a count of none needs an explanation. A far lower rate in those donors.
scenes.visual: Four explanation cards appear. Card one: a lower rate in those donors.
scenes.narration: So a count of none needs an explanation. A far lower rate in those donors.

scenes.tts: A young-neuron protein lost when tissue waited, or was fixed for long.
scenes.visual: Card two: protein lost with time after death or long fixation.
scenes.narration: A young-neuron protein lost when tissue waited, or was fixed for long.

scenes.tts: Or a young state that is short, or unmarked, in people.
scenes.visual: Card three: a short or unmarked young state.
scenes.narration: Or a young state that is short, or unmarked, in people.

scenes.tts: Or sections and stains that missed cells that were there.
scenes.visual: Card four: sampling and detection.
scenes.narration: Or sections and stains that missed cells that were there.

scenes.tts: The human evidence that carries a birth record points to some new neurons.
scenes.visual: The method table: the two birth-record rows, BrdU in patients and carbon-14, highlighted.
scenes.narration: The human evidence that carries a birth record points to some new neurons.

scenes.tts: How many new neurons people make, and what they do, is still open.
scenes.visual: Caption: how many, and what for, still open.
scenes.narration: How many new neurons people make, and what they do, is still open.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: ask whether the same cells carry a birth record and a neuron identity.
scenes.visual: Closing card: birth record plus neuron identity, in the same cells.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: ask whether the same cells carry a birth record and a neuron identity.
